claims.tx: Emotion derives from Middle French émotion (a moving, stirring, agitation) and ultimately from Latin emovēre (to move out, remove, agitate).
Morphologically composed of e- ('out, forth') and movēre ('to move, set in motion'), emotion literally designates a moving-out, a displacement carrying the subject beyond a prior equilibrium.
The modern English noun-forming suffix -ion attached to emovēre names not a static inner feeling but the event of being-moved.
The deeper Indo-European root *meue- ('to push, move, stir') links emotion to motion, momentum, and motivate, reinforcing that its semantic horizon is fundamentally dynamic.
At the level of etymology, emotion mirrors the Aristotelian claim that pathos is a form of kinēsis — being-moved of the soul toward or away from perceived goods and evils.

claims.tx: The single-structure thesis without internal articulational distinction commits one to either of two positions, both of which Aristotle's text resists.
Position 1 (rejected): only the pathē of the Rhetoric count as genuine pathē, and the affective coloring of basic perception is something else — a mere reflex or physiological tone.

Aristotle insists that 'where there is sensation, there is also pleasure and pain,' and the structure he names paschein extends across the entire range of perceptual and rational activity without internal partition.

Position 2 (rejected): the pathē are continuous with basic affective valence in such a way that no real distinction obtains; the determinate emotions of the Rhetoric are simply intensifications of perceptual coloring.

Aristotle's per-emotion analyses (anger, fear, pity) specify propositional contents — the conspicuous slight, the anticipated evil, the undeserved suffering — that the basic affective valence of perception cannot underwrite without doxa-mediation.

The articulational distinction lies in the middle: it preserves the structural unity that the single-structure thesis demands while allowing the differentiated determinacy that Aristotle's per-emotion analyses require.
The unifying ground of the single-structure thesis is the distinction Aristotle draws between two senses of paschein.
In one sense being-affected is a destruction (extinction of one of two contraries by the other).

claims.tx: Basic affective valence is dispositional; it colors the perceptual field with the most general affective tonality of good or bad, pursue or avoid.
The position-taking moment is constitutive of perception with affective valence; it is not introduced anew by doxa.

Basic affective valence satisfies the differentiation aspect pre-propositionally but not pre-positionally — as the perceiver's already-being-disposed toward the perceived as pursue-able or avoid-able — whereas doxa later re-articulates this position-taking propositionally.
The metaballontes aspect is satisfied trivially: 'being pained or pleased, or thinking' are themselves kineseis of the soul; basic affective valence is this kinetic mode at perceptual actualization.
The co-givenness of pleasure and pain is just what basic affective valence is.
Emotion (pathē), by contrast, is more articulationally concrete.
Anger is not undifferentiated displeasure but 'desire accompanied by pain for conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight.'
Each emotion in Aristotle's taxonomy specifies a propositional evaluation, a conative orientation, and a hedonic tonality (the pain or pleasure that attends the whole complex).

Fear's conative orientation is interpretive (Aristotle does not explicitly state it); from the formal structure of avoidance the conative component is the desire to avoid or flee the anticipated/impending evil.
This tripartite determinacy separates emotion from the basic affective valence of pursuit and avoidance.

In each emotion discussed, the desire-component is part of the formal structure: to define what anger is requires mentioning what anger wants.
Desire (orexis) is the moved mover of animal locomotion — the faculty that, moved by the apparent good, moves the animal.

claims.tx: The result is a self-reinforcing recursion: initial doxa concretizes initial pathē; pathē impairs corrective faculty; subsequent phantasmata pass through unopposed; new doxai concretize further pathē; cycle continues until external intervention, somatic exhaustion, or recovery breaks the recursion.

The mechanism renders intelligible a range of phenomena: escalation of anger through sustained rumination, intensification of fear through repeated imagining, susceptibility of the dreamer, the ill, and the passionately agitated to phantasmatic deception.
First structural feature: the loop is not a malfunction of the cognitive system but an intrinsic feature of the relationship between emotion and doxa in rational animals.

Heidegger specifies in Being and Time that state-of-mind (Befindlichkeit) discloses Dasein in three essential respects: in its thrownness; it has already disclosed Being-in-the-world as a whole; and it discloses the worldhood of the world in the mode of circumspective concern.

Thrownness names the diachronic persistence of prior dispositional states: 'we call it the thrownness [Geworfenheit] of this entity into its there; indeed, it is thrown in such a way that, as Being-in-the-world, it is the there.'

Dasein is always already disposed; the disposition is not a contingent psychological state superadded to a pre-existing self but the existential-temporal ground from which any present self-relation takes its bearings.
Heidegger's decisive temporal claim: the Stimmung itself temporalizes primarily in the past-modality of Gewesenheit: 'one's state-of-mind temporalizes itself primarily in having been.'

The having-already-found-itself-disposed of Befindlichkeit is not a past now stored in memory but a Gewesenheit — a having-been — that currently conditions how the entities of the world can come close.
The thrown disposition is operative as the present disclosure's condition, not as a remembered antecedent of it.

The convergence of the Aristotelian and Heideggerian articulations is no mere analogy: it is the recognition of one phenomenon — prior dispositional actualization persists as the ground from which present disclosure takes its character — described at different ontological registers.

claims.tx: The five elements together articulate the generic structure of the pathē; each Aristotelian emotion in the Rhetoric is a specific filling-out of the five — an articulational concretion in which the disposition, the world-side and social-side intentionality, the bodily form, the temporality, and the disclosive function are just so.

The catalog of the Rhetoric is therefore not a list of psychological types but a phenomenology of the determinate ways in which a finite, embodied, speaking being finds itself disposed before the matters that concern it.

Of the five elements, the temporal range bears the chapter's heaviest ontological weight and warrants explicit textual development; the claim that each pathos articulates being-there across all three ecstases has direct warrant in both Aristotle and Heidegger and is not a Heideggerian retrojection.
Aristotle defines memory, perception, and expectation as the three temporal modes of soul's relation to its objects: memory relates to past; perception to present; expectation to future.

Memory and expectation are precisely what phantasia makes possible: 'imagination is a feeble sort of sensation, and memory and expectation involve imagination; therefore things remembered and expected can be pleasant.'
Because phantasia grounds the affective response from doxa and can range across all three temporal modes, every pathos is structurally available to all three ecstases.
Aristotle's per-emotion definitions distribute their primary temporal anchor while preserving traces of all three ecstases.

Fear is lypē tis ē tarachē ek phantasias mellontos kakou — 'pain or disturbance from an imagination of an evil to come'; mellon names the primary futural ecstasis, yet the definition presupposes present tarachē as bodily disquiet and the having-been of the dispositional oiesthai.

Anger is desire accompanied by pain 'for a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight'; the slight has already occurred, the pain is felt now, the revenge is anticipated as future pleasure — 'sweeter by far than the honeycomb' (Aristotle, citing Iliad XVIII.109).

Pity is pain at 'apparent evil befalling one who does not deserve it, and which we might expect to befall ourselves or some friend of ours'; the witnessing is present, production of the suffering reaches back to past causes, phantasmatic projection 'might befall ourselves' opens the futural ecstasis. Shame: aischunē concerns 'bad things, past, present, or future' — Aristotle's own formulation names all three ecstases without remainder.
Heidegger's reading of these passages in GA 18 and his systematic articulation of ecstatic temporality in Being and Time provide the ontological framework recovering what Aristotle has named.

In GA 18 §21, Heidegger glosses fear as 'a disposition that is set before an approaching possibility that pertains to me, comes toward me, and as such announces itself, specifically through the announcement,' concluding that fear discloses the futural character of being-there.

claims.tx: The threefold structure — oiesthai (having-been-dispositioned), tarachē (present-disquiet), phoberon as mellon (futural-threatening) — is Aristotle's own analytic, recovered by Heidegger as the ecstatic temporal articulation of the affect itself.

Being and Time §68 makes the framework general: understanding is primarily futural, state-of-mind primarily grounded in having-been, falling primarily in the present; yet each ecstasis co-temporalizes with the other two.

Fear specifically is analyzed in §68b as 'a bewildered making-present grounded in forgetting that awaits' — a temporal structure braiding together making-present (present-ecstasis of falling), forgetting (having-been-ecstasis of Befindlichkeit in its inauthentic mode), and awaiting (inauthentic-futural-ecstasis of understanding).

The phenomenon of fear is constituted not by a single tense but by the ecstatic unity of all three; the point generalizes to every pathos as a determinate configuration of how the three ecstases co-temporalize in unity.

claims.tx: GA 18 formulates the principle in concentrated form: 'Being itself as care and care-full speech is timely; it cares for the still-not-at-hand, speaks about the already-appeared, investigates that which is now with us.'

The three rhetorical genres — deliberative (futural), forensic (having-been), epideictic (present) — correspond to these three temporal orientations; the architecture of the Rhetoric operationalizes the temporal range the pathē concretize.

What Struever names Alltäglichkeit as 'timefulness' — the radical specificity of time, the care for tense that defines practical life — is not an external imposition on the pathē but their own internal temporal articulation made explicit.

claims.tx: Rhetoric is the cultivation of the dispositional ground that brings being-there to discourse; Aristotle's Rhetoric is therefore not a manual of persuasion-techniques but a phenomenology of the disclosive structures through which being-there finds itself in the polis.

The pathē are not psychological phenomena to be added to a prior account of cognition; they are the prior — the modes in which being-there has its world disclosed, on the basis of which cognition and speaking become possible.

Heidegger's retrospective citation of the Rhetoric as 'the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being-with-one-another' is not a passing historical note but a precise diagnostic: the Rhetoric's catalog of pathē is the first sustained phenomenology of mood, and GA 18 is the preparatory work in which that phenomenology is recovered for the Befindlichkeit-analytic of Being and Time.
The pathē are co-original with hexeis: both are fundamental concepts of being, articulating the being-structure of beings whose way of being is '******' (BCAP, p. ******).

claims.tx: Hexeis are what consolidate over time through repeated actualization of pathos-chains, so that the present pathos is always shaped by the dispositional ground that prior actualizations have sedimented.

Emotion responds to appearance, not to corrected judgment; if phantasia supplies the appearance, doxa is the moment of apophantic assertion — taking-something-as-true; the pathos that follows is a being-moved keyed to the appearance, not to whatever subsequent rational correction may apply.

The sound mistaken for a rattlesnake produces real fear, even though the corrected judgment will dissolve the mistake; false beliefs generate real emotions because emotion is keyed to the phantasmatic appearance, not to its eventual correction.
Art produces emotion, because phantasmatic representation suffices to occasion the affective movement, even when the audience knows the represented event is unreal.

claims.tx: Emotion can contradict subsequent judgment, as when knowing the rope is not a snake fails to neutralize the startle, because rational correction does not unwind the prior phantasmatic-doxastic uptake on which the affective movement was built.

Phantasia generates appearances beyond the immediately present, so the temporal depth of emotional life follows directly; Aristotle in De Memoria: 'the movement caused by the object is preserved internally.'

To remember grief is to feel grief again; to anticipate pleasure is to feel pleasure now in relation to a not-yet. Aristotle: 'both the man who remembers and the man who hopes will be attended by an imagination of what he remembers or hopes.'

claims.tx: Fear paradigmatically is 'a pain or disturbance due to imagining some destructive or painful evil in the future'; the feared event does not exist, the phantasma does, and the soul moves as though the feared thing were present.

Phantasia is not a decorative adjunct to emotion; it is the condition of possibility for the soul's being-moved by absences, possibilities, appearances, and counterfactuals — the condition of possibility for the entire range of higher-order pathē.

To persuade is not primarily to offer proofs but to reshape the listener's phantasmatic field; the rhetor must supply images — concrete, narrative, affectively charged — that allow the audience to see what the rhetor wants them to see, since this imagistic seeing grounds the subsequent formation of doxa, the ensuing movement of emotion, and the eventual act of judgment.

claims.tx: For Aristotle, emotion is the kinetic, affective, evaluative dimension of how the world appears to a finite, embodied, speaking being; grounded in phantasia, shaped through involuntary doxa, felt as pleasure or pain, prepared somatically, expressed as motion toward or away from what the soul takes to be significant.

Emotion is not an add-on to rationality, nor a disruption of cognition, nor a mere physiological disturbance, but the way the soul's self-movement discloses significance at all; the five-fold structure — disposition, intentionality, bodily form, temporal range, disclosive function — specifies the architecture of this disclosure for each of the determinate pathē the Rhetoric catalogs; emotion in its full Aristotelian sense is the affective architecture of being-in-the-world.

The cultivation of the hexeis corresponding to each pathos — the practical-ethical task of shaping one's dispositional ground over time — is the subject of the next chapter, where the temporal sedimentation specified in §1.7 receives sustained practical-philosophical treatment.
